messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Retail Worker
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 59

He is thirty-six, European, married, and works on the late shift at a large home-goods store on the edge of town. When he talks about what happened, he does not begin with the fire itself. He begins with the ordinary parts of that day, as if his mind still wants to prove that it started like any other. He remembers restocking kettles and boxed lamps, joking with a coworker about a broken pallet jack, texting his wife to ask if they needed milk. It is near closing when the first alarm sounds. At first, no one moves quickly. False alarms happen. Then he smells something chemical and sharp, and a customer starts shouting from the stockroom corridor.

The fire spreads faster than he can make sense of it. Later he learns it was caused deliberately, set by a man who had been banned from the store after a fight with management. In the moment, all he knows is that the back hallway fills with smoke and the emergency lights cast everything in a strange red pulse. He runs toward the front, then turns back when he realizes two customers are still in the appliance aisle. For years he has thought of himself as an ordinary man, not especially brave, but that night his body moves before he can think. He grabs one elderly customer by the arm, yells for another to follow, and pushes through heat that feels unreal, like opening an oven door onto his whole face and chest.

Outside, in the parking lot, he is coughing so hard he vomits. He can hear glass breaking somewhere inside. He keeps counting heads, looking for coworkers, certain he has forgotten someone. One of the younger staff members is crying and asking where the assistant manager is. He remembers trying to go back in and being held back by firefighters. The assistant manager does not make it out. For months afterward, this becomes the fixed point in his memory: not the flames, but the sensation of being restrained while the building burns and feeling, with absolute conviction, that he is abandoning someone.

In the first weeks after, everyone tells him he is lucky. News coverage calls employees heroes. His wife says she is grateful he is alive. He nods because these things are true, but he feels oddly cut off from them. Sleep changes first. He jerks awake after an hour or two, heart pounding, sure he smells smoke. Sometimes he dreams he is trapped in the stockroom and cannot find the exit; sometimes he sees his assistant manager standing calmly in aisle fourteen as the ceiling darkens above him. On better nights he does not dream at all, but he lies rigid beside his wife, listening for alarms, sirens, the hum of faulty wiring.

He returns to work when the store reopens in a temporary location, though he dreads it long before his first shift. The new building is bright and modern, but he notices every fire exit the second he walks in. He insists on keeping the stockroom door propped open. When customers linger too long in the aisles near closing, he feels irritation rise out of proportion to the moment, a hot, immediate anger that embarrasses him. If someone drops a metal cart or a child screams unexpectedly, his whole body jolts. Coworkers laugh it off—“still twitchy, mate?”—and he forces a smile, but afterward he is shaky and ashamed.

At home, his world gets smaller. Before, he and his wife used to go into the city on weekends, meet friends, wander through crowded markets. Now he avoids cinemas, concerts, anywhere doors feel far away. He chooses restaurants based on how visible the exits are. On bad days he circles the block before going into any building. His wife notices that he sits facing the door, that he checks the hob twice before bed, that he gets up in the night to make sure the plug sockets are off. When she asks what he is doing, he says, “Just checking,” in a tone that ends the conversation.

He does not talk much about the dead manager, but guilt sits beneath almost everything he says. He remembers small details about the man—how he always carried mints, how he was fussy about folded receipts—and these details ambush him at work. The smell of scorched plastic from a broken toaster return can ruin an entire shift. He finds himself staring at customers’ faces without hearing what they are saying. Sometimes he loses track of simple tasks, scanning the same item twice or forgetting why he walked into the storeroom. He used to be patient with difficult customers; now he feels his chest tighten and his jaw clench when someone raises their voice.

His wife tells him he is present and absent at the same time. He sits beside her on the sofa but startles when she touches his shoulder. He loves her, he says that clearly, yet he avoids intimacy on nights when he feels wound tight and untouchable. There are evenings when he drinks two or three beers not to enjoy them, but to flatten the edges of the night enough that sleep might come. Even then, he wakes before dawn and lies there with the old counting ritual in his head—staff, customers, exits, alarms—trying to prevent, after the fact, something that has already happened.
